questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how a Permission Set relates to a Profile in Salesforce?
options: A permission set can grant additional access on top of a user's profile, but it can never take away access the profile already grants.
A permission set can grant additional access on top of a user's profile, and can also revoke specific permissions the profile grants, which is why assigning one needs careful review.
A permission set replaces a user's profile entirely once it's assigned, becoming their new baseline permissions.
A user can hold at most one permission set in addition to their profile — a second one requires a permission set group instead.
A permission set only takes effect if the user's profile grants no object permissions at all for that object.
A permission set and its user's profile must always share the exact same User License, or Salesforce rejects the assignment outright.
questions.explain: A permission set is a grant-only container: it layers extra object permissions, field-level security, app visibility, or system permissions on top of whatever a user's one mandatory profile already grants, but it can never remove or override access the profile provides. That's also why assigning one is low-risk — it cannot accidentally lock a user out of anything.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B restates the same relationship almost word for word, but reverses the single most important rule from Lesson 6: a permission set only ever adds access, it never revokes it. If permission sets could revoke a profile's grants, assigning one would carry the same risk as editing the profile directly — which is exactly the risk the grant-only design is built to avoid.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Network Access versus profile-level Login IP Ranges, per Lesson 8.
options: Network Access is configured org-wide; Login IP Ranges is configured per profile.
A login from outside the org's Network Access trusted range is blocked outright, with no fallback.
A login from outside a profile's Login IP Ranges is blocked entirely, with no verification-code fallback.
Both settings, when violated, trigger the exact same identity-verification flow.
Login IP Ranges lives inside the Profile record, the same place Login Hours lives.
questions.explain: Network Access is an org-wide trusted-IP setting; a login from outside it isn't blocked, it just triggers Salesforce's identity-verification flow (a code sent to the user). Login IP Ranges is a stricter, profile-level setting: a login from outside the range is refused outright, with no verification fallback at all. Login IP Ranges and Login Hours both live inside the same Profile record.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on the New User form, ________ must be selected before Profile, because it determines which profiles even appear in that dropdown.
questions.explain: User License sits directly above Profile on the New User form because the relationship is a real dependency, not a layout choice — each license type only works with a matching subset of profiles, so picking the license first determines what Profile even offers.

questions.prompt: Match each login-control setting to what it actually governs, per Lesson 8.
right: Org-wide setting controlling whether admins can log in as other users without the user granting access first
Org-wide trusted IP ranges; a login from outside triggers identity verification, not a block
Profile-level restriction on which days and times a user with that profile may log in at all
Profile-level IP restriction; a login from outside is blocked entirely, with no fallback
questions.explain: Login Access Policies and Network Access are both org-wide: one governs admin login-as, the other governs trusted IPs with a verification fallback. Login Hours and Login IP Ranges both live inside the Profile record: one restricts by day/time, the other blocks outright by IP with no fallback.

questions.prompt: An admin wants to let a regional office manager create and edit users within their own role hierarchy, but is worried the manager could assign a new hire the System Administrator profile. Which setting specifically closes that gap?
options: Assignable Profiles — the explicit list of profiles the delegated group's members are permitted to assign
User Administration scope — the roles and subordinates the delegated group can create and edit users within
Enable Group for Login Access — lets members log in as the users they administer
Custom Object Administration — which custom objects the group can fully administer
questions.explain: User Administration scope controls which users a delegated admin can create and edit, but creating a user still means assigning them a profile. Assignable Profiles is the separate guardrail that limits which profiles can actually be handed out — anything not on that list simply isn't offered, closing the exact gap the manager is worried about.

questions.prompt: A permission set group includes a permission set that grants Delete access on Opportunities. The admin mutes that Delete permission inside the group. What happens when that same permission set is used on its own, outside this group?
options: It still grants Delete access on Opportunities normally — muting only suppresses the permission inside this one group's combined result
Delete access is muted everywhere the permission set is used, in every group and as a standalone assignment
The permission set is automatically removed from the group once muted
The group's status flips to Outdated because of the mute, until Salesforce recalculates it
questions.explain: Muting is scoped only to the group doing the muting. The underlying permission set is untouched — assigned standalone, or used in a different group, it still grants Delete on Opportunities exactly as built.

questions.prompt: An admin tries to permanently delete a departed employee's user record. What actually happens, and why?
options: Salesforce refuses — a user record can only be deactivated, never deleted, because deleting it would orphan every record they own, every report crediting them, and the audit trail
It succeeds, and every record the user owned is deleted along with them
It succeeds, immediately freeing their license seat, but all of their historically owned records become ownerless
It only works if the user was frozen first, as a required first step
questions.explain: Salesforce never lets you delete a user record. The record is tied to everything that user ever touched — record ownership, report authorship, audit trail entries — so the only supported offboarding path is deactivation, which removes login access while leaving the record and its history fully intact.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of getting a brand-new hire set up with Salesforce access, per Chapter 1, in the correct order.
items: Choose the User License the org has a seat for
Select a Profile compatible with that license
Save the user record with Active checked, triggering a welcome email
Assign any additional Permission Sets the role specifically needs
Check User Access Summary to confirm the final access actually matches what was intended
questions.explain: License comes first because it filters which profiles are even available. Profile sets the baseline, and saving an Active user with the welcome-email option sends the login link. Permission sets layer on afterward for anything the profile alone doesn't cover. User Access Summary is the final check that the combined result — license, profile, and permission sets together — actually grants what was intended.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Permission Set Groups, per Lesson 7.
options: A group's 'Outdated' status means a member permission set changed and the group's combined access needs to be recalculated
Muting a permission inside a group permanently removes that permission from the underlying permission set everywhere it's used
A permission set group can be assigned to, and later removed from, users as a single unit
Permission set groups exist so that one permission set can be reused across multiple separate assignments
Recalculation of an Outdated group's combined access typically happens automatically, within minutes
questions.explain: Outdated means a member set changed and the group's combined result needs recalculating, which Salesforce normally does automatically within minutes. The whole point of a group is bundling several permission sets into one assignable, removable unit. Muting is scoped to the group only — it never touches the underlying permission set itself.

questions.prompt: An org has 'US Support Hours' and 'EMEA Support Hours' as two separate Business Hours records. An admin creates one Holiday for December 25th but attaches it only to US Support Hours. What happens for EMEA Support Hours on that date?
options: EMEA Support Hours treats December 25th as a normal business day, because a holiday only suspends the Business Hours records it's explicitly attached to
EMEA Support Hours automatically closes too, since holidays apply org-wide the moment they're created
The holiday is rejected at save time, because it must be attached to every Business Hours record in the org
EMEA Support Hours closes only if its time zone happens to match US Support Hours's time zone
questions.explain: A holiday does nothing on its own — it only suspends the specific Business Hours records it's associated with, via that record's own Business Hours related list. Attaching it to just one record leaves every other Business Hours record, including EMEA Support Hours, running its normal weekly schedule on that date.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once a currency is marked Active in a multi-currency org, it can never be ________ — only deactivated.
questions.explain: Activation is a one-way door for a currency: once active, it can be deactivated later but never deleted outright — which is exactly why the Currency Setup page warns against activating currencies 'just in case' before they're actually needed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Fiscal Year and Multiple Currencies, per Lesson 13.
options: A Standard Fiscal Year is defined just by picking a start month and how the fiscal year is named
A Custom Fiscal Year can be turned back off once enabled, restoring Standard Fiscal Year behavior
Changing an existing org's fiscal year start month affects opportunities and forecasts organization-wide
Activating Multiple Currencies automatically changes the org's corporate currency to whichever currency is activated first
A Custom Fiscal Year is typically used for non-calendar patterns, like a 4-4-5 week retail calendar
questions.explain: Standard Fiscal Year just needs a start month and a naming convention. Shifting the start month on an existing org moves every fiscal period forward and affects forecasts org-wide, which is why the setup page recommends exporting data first. Custom Fiscal Year exists for non-calendar patterns like 4-4-5 weeks, but once enabled it cannot be disabled again. Activating Multiple Currencies doesn't touch the corporate currency at all — it only adds the ability to mark additional currencies Active alongside it.

questions.prompt: Match each New Lightning App wizard step to what it actually configures.
right: The icon image and highlight color shown for the app in the App Launcher
Navigation style (Standard vs. Console) and supported form factors
Docked footer tools like Notes, Recent Items, or a softphone
Which tabs appear in the app, and in what order
Which profiles can see and open the app at all
questions.explain: The wizard's five steps each own one slice of app configuration: branding is purely visual, App Options sets the navigation style, Utility Items configures the docked footer, Navigation Items sets the tab set and order, and User Profiles gates which profiles can even see the app.

questions.prompt: A support manager wants agents to see a case, its contact, and its account all open at once, without losing their place when jumping between them. Which App Options setting enables that, and why?
options: Console navigation — it opens records as subtabs inside one workspace tab, so an agent can jump between them without losing their place
Standard navigation — each record opens in its own separate tab, keeping everything cleanly organized
The Utility Bar — docking the case, contact, and account as utility items keeps all three open at once
This isn't controlled by Navigation Style at all; it comes from the page layout instead
questions.explain: Console navigation is built exactly for this: it opens records as subtabs inside a single workspace tab, letting an agent jump between a case, its contact, and its account without reloading the page or losing their current spot. Standard navigation is the single-record-at-a-time experience Console is specifically an alternative to.

questions.prompt: An org has a custom Record Page assigned as the App Default for the Sales app, and a different custom Record Page assigned at the App, Record Type, and Profile level for that same app and a specific profile. Which page does a user with that profile actually see?
options: The App, Record Type, and Profile page — it's the most specific assignment level and overrides the App Default
The App Default page, since it was configured before the more specific one
Both pages render stacked on the same screen, one above the other
The Org Default page, since it always takes priority over any app-specific assignment
questions.explain: Lightning page assignment resolves across three levels — Org Default, App Default, and App/Record Type/Profile — with each one overriding the one before it. The most specific level always wins, so a user matching the App/Record Type/Profile assignment sees that page, not the App Default.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Field History Tracking's field-count limits is correct?
options: Most objects can track up to 20 fields, but Tasks and Events are capped at 6 tracked fields each
Most objects can track up to 20 fields, and Tasks and Events share that same 20-field limit since they're standard objects too
Every object, without exception, is capped at 6 tracked fields unless the paid Field Audit Trail add-on is purchased
Tracked fields are unlimited by default; exceeding 20 only slows down page load times, it doesn't block anything
Most objects can track up to 60 fields, with Tasks and Events capped at 20
Field History Tracking has no field-count limit at all; the only limit is how long history is retained
questions.explain: Most standard and custom objects can track up to 20 fields each, a limit most orgs never hit. Tasks and Events are the specific exception, capped at a noticeably tighter 6 tracked fields — a detail that catches admins off guard if they assume every object behaves the same way.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the general 20-field limit right, which makes it the closest wrong answer, but it drops the one exception the lesson calls out by name: Tasks and Events are capped at 6, not 20, specifically because they're the objects experienced admins get caught off guard by.

questions.prompt: A record's Details tab shows a dozen fields from its page layout, but its highlights panel at the top shows only three. Why doesn't the highlights panel grow when the page layout gains more fields?
options: The highlights panel is driven by a separate, deliberately small configuration — the compact layout — not the page layout
The highlights panel is hard-capped by Salesforce at exactly three fields and can never show more
The page layout's extra fields are duplicates that the system filters out of the highlights panel automatically
The compact layout automatically mirrors the page layout's first three fields, so it should change too if the page layout does
questions.explain: The highlights panel is driven entirely by the compact layout, a short and separate configuration from the page layout. Adding fields to the page layout has no effect on it at all — only editing the compact layout's own Selected Fields changes what appears up top.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Record Types and Business Processes, per Lesson 20.
options: A record type can control which page layout a user with a given profile sees
Case, Lead, and Opportunity record types each require an associated process restricting a key picklist's values
Every object's record types require an associated business process, not just Case, Lead, and Opportunity
A record type can control which profiles are even allowed to create a record of that type
Cloning an existing record type during creation is the only way a record type's picklist values can ever be changed afterward
questions.explain: A record type bundles several things together: which page layout a profile sees for that record type, which profiles can create it at all, and — specifically for Case, Lead, and Opportunity — an associated process restricting the key status/stage picklist. That process requirement is specific to those three objects, not universal, and a record type's picklist values can still be adjusted after creation, not only set once at cloning time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a field dependency, the field a user picks first — the one that filters another field's available values — is called the ________ field.
questions.explain: The controlling field is what a user picks first; the dependent field's available values are then filtered based on that pick. Issue Type controlling Issue Detail is the lesson's example of this relationship.

questions.prompt: A 'Region' global value set is used by a picklist field on both Lead and Contact. An admin adds a new value, 'Antarctica', directly to the global value set. Does the admin need to separately add it to each object's picklist field?
options: No — every field pointed at that global value set automatically shares the same list, so adding it once there is enough
Yes, each object's field keeps its own independent copy of the values once the field is created
Only if 'Restrict picklist to the values defined in the value set' was left unchecked on both fields
Yes, but only for custom objects — standard objects like Lead and Contact need the value added manually
questions.explain: The entire point of a global value set is a single source of truth: the values are defined once, and every field across every object that points at that same value set shares it automatically. Adding a value once at the global value set is sufficient — there's no separate per-object copy to update.

questions.prompt: An Account has 40 closed-lost Opportunities and 3 open ones, all shown together in one related list, burying the open deals a rep actually needs today. What's the correct fix, per Lesson 25?
options: Replace the standard related list with a Dynamic Related List filtered to Stage is not Closed
Build a separate report filtered to open Opportunities and link to it from the record page
Ask reps to manually sort the related list by Stage every time they open the record
Turn on Field History Tracking on the Stage field so reps can see which Opportunities changed recently
questions.explain: A standard related list shows every related record with no filtering of its own. A Dynamic Related List adds exactly the filtering needed here — showing only the open Opportunities directly on the record page, with no separate report and no manual sorting required.

questions.prompt: A user says a field that's visible as a column in a list view returns nothing when typed into that list view's own search box. What's the most likely explanation?
options: That field isn't indexed for in-list search — filters or sorting, not the search box, are the right tool for it
The list view has a typo in one of its saved filter conditions
The field needs Field History Tracking turned on before it can be searched
In-list search only works for fields that are also part of the object's compact layout
questions.explain: Not every column shown in a list view is indexed for the list's own in-list search — system fields like Created Date are common examples. Salesforce tells the user this directly with a tooltip and points them at filters or sorting instead, since those operate differently from the typed search box.

questions.prompt: A new hire can't see the 'Edit in Builder' button on an Email Template, while a long-tenured colleague can. What's the most likely cause?
options: The colleague has a permission set granting 'Access drag-and-drop content builder,' which the new hire hasn't been assigned yet
The new hire's user license doesn't support email at all
Edit in Builder only appears after 24 hours have passed since the user's account was created
Email Templates is a custom object that first needs to be deployed into the org with a change set
questions.explain: The modern drag-and-drop Email Template Builder isn't on by default — it requires the 'Access drag-and-drop content builder' system permission, granted through a permission set. A user without that permission set is stuck with the older, plainer template editor and never sees Edit in Builder.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Email-to-Case, per Lesson 27.
options: Once Enable Email-to-Case is turned on, it cannot be disabled again later
The routing address's real email address (like support@yourcompany.com) is what Salesforce directly receives inbound mail at
Insert Thread ID lets a customer's reply get matched back to the correct existing case instead of creating a new one
On-Demand Service requires installing on-premise software to receive inbound mail
Case Owner, Priority, and Origin can be set as defaults directly on the routing address
questions.explain: Enable Email-to-Case is a one-way door — once on, it can't be turned back off. Thread ID is exactly how a reply gets matched to its original case instead of spawning a duplicate. Routing addresses carry their own Case Owner/Priority/Origin defaults. What Salesforce actually receives mail at is the generated, unguessable *.case.salesforce.com address — the real inbox only forwards to it. On-Demand Service is the modern, no-local-software delivery method; the legacy Email-to-Case Agent is the one requiring on-premise software.

questions.prompt: A Flow runs a 'Send Custom Notification' action referencing a Custom Notification Type that has only the Desktop channel enabled. What happens on that user's phone when the Flow fires?
options: Nothing reaches the phone — since Mobile isn't an enabled channel for this notification type, only the in-app bell gets the notification
It still pushes to the phone, since every Custom Notification reaches every channel by default
It's sent as an Email Alert instead, as an automatic fallback
The Flow fails to run entirely, because Desktop-only notification types require an Apex trigger
questions.explain: Supported Channels is set per Custom Notification Type at creation — Desktop, Mobile, or both. A type with only Desktop enabled never reaches the mobile app, no matter how the Flow fires it; the notification still badges the bell, but nothing pushes to the phone.

questions.prompt: An Opportunity's Amount field has both Feed Tracking and Field History Tracking turned on. A sales manager wants a permanent, queryable record of exactly who changed the Amount and when. Which feature actually gives them that, and why?
options: Field History Tracking — Feed Tracking is a social post to the record's Chatter feed, not a long-term audit record in the same way
Feed Tracking — it posts the moment a change happens, which is more immediate
Either one equally, since both record the exact same information in the exact same place
Neither — a permanent record of field changes always requires the paid Field Audit Trail add-on
questions.explain: Feed Tracking auto-posts a change to the record's Chatter feed — useful for visibility, but it's a social post, not a structured audit record. Field History Tracking is the feature that writes the old value, new value, date, and user into the object's History related list, which is what actually answers 'who changed this, and when.'

questions.prompt: Match each sandbox type to what it actually includes, per Lesson 31.
right: 200 MB storage, metadata only, no production records
1 GB storage, metadata only, for larger in-progress projects
5 GB storage, a sampled subset of real data chosen via a Sandbox Template
Storage matching production, including all production data
questions.explain: Developer and Developer Pro both copy metadata only, differing just in storage size. Partial Copy adds a sampled slice of real data defined by a Sandbox Template. Full matches production in both storage and data, making it the choice for staging and final sign-off.

questions.prompt: A change set containing only a new custom field and a page layout update — no Apex classes or triggers — is ready to deploy to production. Which Apex test-coverage requirement actually applies?
options: None of the Apex test-coverage requirements apply, since the change set contains no Apex components at all
Run All Tests must be selected regardless of what the change set contains
75% code coverage is still required, because every production deployment requires it regardless of content
The deployment is blocked until a Sandbox Template is created for it first
questions.explain: The 75% code coverage requirement and the choice of test level only come into play when a change set actually includes Apex classes or triggers. A change set with just a field and a page layout has nothing for Apex tests to run against, so that requirement simply doesn't apply.

questions.prompt: A user reports a Flow stopped working, and the admin suspects someone changed a validation rule by accident. Which tool actually answers that question, and why?
options: Setup Audit Trail — it records configuration changes, including who edited a validation rule and when
Login History — it would show who was logged into the org at the time
Field History Tracking — validation rules are a field-level setting, so this is the right tool
Either Setup Audit Trail or Login History works equally well for this question
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail answers 'who changed this setting' — exactly the question here, since a validation rule is a configuration change, not a record-data change or a login event. Login History only shows login attempts, and Field History Tracking covers changes to record data, not org configuration like validation rules.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the change-management loop, per Lesson 35, in the correct order.
items: Build and test the change in a sandbox
Move the validated change into production with a Change Set
Watch for Release Updates that might interact with the newly deployed change
Check Setup Audit Trail and Login History afterward if anything looks off
questions.explain: The loop runs test-first: a sandbox is where mistakes cost nothing, a Change Set is the deliberate, reviewed way the tested work actually reaches production, Release Updates are watched because a platform behavior shift can interact with what just deployed, and the audit tools are the fallback for confirming exactly what happened if something still looks wrong afterward.
